content: Telephone triage refers to the process of managing patients' health concerns and symptoms through telephone communication, typically conducted by advice nurses. This practice predates telemedicine and telehealth, as it relies on traditional telephone lines. Telehealth, on the other hand, encompasses the delivery of health-related services and information through telecommunications technologies and serves as an umbrella term for all variations of healthcare services provided via such technologies. In telephone triage, nurses use established protocols or guidelines, available in either paper or electronic formats, to assess and prioritize symptoms ranging from chest pain to chickenpox. The process involves ranking the urgency of patients' health issues, educating and advising them, and making safe, effective, and appropriate decisions—all conducted over the phone. This practice spans a wide range of applications, including disease management, AIDS counseling, child abuse hotlines, 911 services, and telemetry monitoring. It is utilized in diverse settings such as emergency rooms, large call centers, and hospices. Telephone triage nurses, also known as advice nurses, telepractitioners, telenurses, telepractice nurses, or consulting nurses, handle a high volume of calls during their shifts. For example, a telenurse may manage 60-80 calls in an 8-hour shift, addressing issues such as headaches, newborn rashes, chest pain, potential allergic reactions, medication inquiries, and seasonal flu symptoms. They may also guide patients to seek second medical opinions or direct them to reliable health information sources. In some cases, they provide crisis intervention, such as counseling individuals at risk of suicide. What was once an informal practice in emergency rooms, clinics, and physicians' offices has evolved into a recognized nursing subspecialty known as telephone triage. Telenurses work in various settings, including large medical call centers, physicians' offices, clinics, hospices, college health centers, disease management call centers, poison control centers, and emergency departments. The nature of their work often involves uncertainty, as decisions are made based on incomplete or inaccurate information, and urgency, as calls must be processed within a short timeframe, typically 6-10 minutes. Research has likened telephone triage to high-stakes professions such as air traffic controllers, emergency medical dispatchers, and firefighters. Nurses in this field rely on strategies like pattern recognition, rules of thumb, and contextual understanding to make real-world decisions. Protocols or guidelines serve as standing orders for nurses to assess and manage a range of symptoms. These protocols may be viewed as decision-making tools or decision-support tools, and their design is a topic of ongoing debate. Research on nurse decision-making highlights the importance of incorporating strategies like pattern recognition, rules of thumb, and context into decision-support systems, training, and documentation forms. The goal is to emulate the brain's natural problem-solving processes in real-world situations. Telephone triage is a high-risk area of practice because nurses cannot physically see the patients they are assisting. Therefore, training and guidelines are essential to support nurses in this role. Over-reliance on protocols without formal instruction can lead to errors, such as mis-triage. The best approach combines experience, specialized training, and robust decision-support tools. Proper training in the safe use of protocols and documentation can help prevent misunderstandings and errors. Historically, informal telephone triage dates back to the invention of the telephone itself. One of Alexander Graham Bell's first calls was for assistance following a battery acid burn. Physicians quickly adopted telephones in their practices, recognizing their utility. Initially, physicians provided telephone advice, but by the 1970s, health maintenance organizations began employing nurses to fulfill this role. The term telephone triage was formally recognized in 1990, marking the emergence of this subspecialty. In the early days of telephone triage, there were few job qualifications, and most nurses were considered qualified. However, as the field evolved, it became clear that the high-stakes, high-stress nature of the work required experienced registered nurses (RNs) with years of bedside decision-making experience. New graduates were generally not considered ideal candidates for telephone triage, as less experience often led to over-triage, while more experience resulted in more appropriate decisions. Typically, 5-10 years of experience provide the foundation necessary for effective decision-making in this challenging role. RNs are preferred for their autonomy and cost-effectiveness, as they are the lowest-paid professionals capable of safely performing the job. Telephone triage demands excellent interpersonal skills, or telephone charisma, as well as a calm, mature, and patient temperament. Computer literacy is also desirable. Training in telephone triage has evolved from informal, on-the-job learning to formal programs. In the 1990s, structured training programs emerged, with the best programs requiring a minimum of 40 hours. Orientation covers an overview of the field, the nursing role, communication skills, history-taking, interview and documentation skills, protocol use, and medical-legal aspects. Training methods include reading, lectures, discussions, shadowing, written exercises, audiotape analysis, preceptor programs, and role-playing mock calls. Role-playing is particularly effective for integrating new skills and simulating real tasks. Preceptors provide support and guidance to new advice nurses during their first 3-6 months. National conferences offer opportunities for networking and problem-solving, and since 1994, telephone triage conferences have provided a platform for sharing expertise. The future of telepractice may involve high-tech, high-volume call centers operating 24/7. Job descriptions for telenurses may require extensive nursing and telephone triage experience, computer literacy, cultural sensitivity, and excellent communication skills. Experience with telemedicine and telemetry may also be necessary. Training programs will likely include online modules and patient call simulations, with a focus on real-life scenarios. Accreditation, anticipated within the next 5-10 years, will formalize the field further. Future conferences will likely be international, fostering collaboration and knowledge-sharing across cultures and nations. In the future, telehealth will integrate telephone triage with visual displays, telemonitoring, and internet access for both nurses and patients. Home health assessments may include heart, lung, and bowel sounds, blood pressure and pulse readings, gait analysis, neurological exams, and mood assessments. Nurses will be cross-trained to monitor various health parameters and manage conditions like congestive heart failure, asthma, and diabetes. They may also serve as community sentinels, alerting agencies to public health threats. As telehealth continues to evolve, advice nurses will become experts in chronobiology, understanding how biorhythms affect health and predicting seasonal and diurnal surges in conditions like allergic reactions, heart attacks, and strokes.
